1.modern-en: Marlow begins his story on the deck of the Nellie, anchored in the Thames at dusk. He tells his companions about securing a steamboat command through his aunt's connections, traveling to the Company's Brussels office, and arriving at the African coast. At the Outer Station he witnesses chained laborers and dying men in a grove. He meets the impeccable Chief Accountant, who first mentions Kurtz. He treks overland to the Central Station, where he finds his steamboat sunk and learns it will take months to repair.

2.modern-en: Marlow overhears the Manager and his uncle discussing Kurtz and the threat he poses to their positions. He focuses on repairing the steamboat, frustrated by the months-long wait for rivets. When the journey upriver finally begins, the steamer pushes through fog and narrowing channels. Near Kurtz's station the boat is attacked from the bank, and Marlow's helmsman is killed by a spear.

3.modern-en: Marlow meets the Russian trader who has been living near Kurtz, and then Kurtz himself — emaciated, dying, and carried out on a stretcher. He discovers the severed heads on stakes around the station. During the night Kurtz crawls from the steamer toward a fire in the bush, and Marlow follows and confronts him. On the journey downriver Kurtz dies, his last words 'The horror! The horror!' Marlow falls ill himself. Back in Brussels a year later, he visits the Intended and lies to her about Kurtz's final words.

1.modern-en: Kurtz is mentioned but never seen. The Chief Accountant at the Outer Station describes him as a first-class agent who sends in more ivory than all the others combined. At the Central Station, Marlow hears more about him — a man of remarkable talents who is expected to go very far in the Company. Kurtz exists in this chapter only as reputation and rumor.

2.modern-en: Kurtz remains offstage but dominates every conversation. The Manager and his uncle discuss him as a threat to their careers. Marlow finds a note from Kurtz downriver that reads 'Hurry up. Approach cautiously.' The attack on the steamer may be connected to Kurtz's people trying to prevent his removal. The Russian trader, encountered at the end, is the first person to speak of Kurtz with genuine devotion.

3.modern-en: Kurtz finally appears: skeletal, carried on a stretcher, surrounded by worshipping followers and severed heads. He speaks eloquently and grandly even while dying. During the night he escapes the steamer and crawls toward a fire, and Marlow brings him back. On the downriver journey he entrusts Marlow with his papers and a photograph of the Intended. He dies pronouncing 'The horror! The horror!' — words Marlow later calls a moral victory, though the text leaves this ambiguous.

1.modern-en: The Manager greets Marlow at the Central Station and informs him that the steamboat has been sunk. He speaks about Kurtz with an unease that Marlow interprets as jealousy. He has no remarkable qualities except an ability to survive the climate and an instinct for making others uneasy.

2.modern-en: Marlow overhears the Manager talking with his uncle about Kurtz, revealing his hope that the climate will eliminate a rival. He accompanies the upriver journey and reacts to the attack with self-serving alarm, blaming the delay on 'this miserable trader' at the Inner Station.

3.modern-en: The Manager arrives at Kurtz's station and surveys the scene with satisfaction, remarking that Kurtz's methods are 'unsound.' Marlow realizes the Manager is glad Kurtz is dying because it removes a competitor. When Kurtz dies, the Manager takes charge of the ivory.

2.modern-en: The Russian is first detected indirectly — a stack of firewood left with a note, and a book on seamanship annotated in what turns out to be cipher (actually Russian). Marlow encounters him at the end of the chapter near Kurtz's station.

3.modern-en: The Russian appears in his patched, multicolored clothes and explains his devotion to Kurtz with breathless enthusiasm. He tells Marlow about Kurtz's powers, his hold over the local people, and the raids for ivory. He admits that Kurtz threatened to shoot him once over a small lot of ivory. Marlow advises him to leave before the Manager can move against him, and the Russian slips away into the forest.

Marlow visits the Intended in Brussels more than a year after Kurtz's death. She is still in mourning, living in an atmosphere of preserved grief. She asks Marlow to tell her Kurtz's last words. Marlow, unable to shatter her idealized memory, lies and says the last word Kurtz spoke was her name. It is the novella's final act — a mercy and a betrayal in the same sentence.
